title: The interplay between additive and symmetric large sets and their combinatorial applications

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The formula is written as e_j(X_1,…,X_n)=\sum_{1\le i_1\le\cdots\le i_j\le n}X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_j}=\sum_{\emptyset\ne G\subseteq\{1,…,n\}}\prod_{s\in G}X_s. Both expressions are wrong: the indices must be strictly increasing (i_1<\cdots<i_j), otherwise repeated variables occur, and the set-version must run over subsets G with |G|=j, not over all nonempty G (the sum over all nonempty G equals \sum_j e_j, not e_j).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2, sentence after the display for \prod_{j=1}^n(la_j+k)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "If k,l∈N, then c∈Z if and only if l | k(k-1)" is false as an equivalence for general n: c∈Z iff l | k^n−k. Counterexample: l=7, k=2, n=4 gives k^n−k=14 divisible by 7 (so c∈Z) while k(k−1)=2 is not divisible by 7.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2 (after Definition 2.6) and Section 4.2 opening paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "It is easy to verify that (Z, ⊙_{l,k}) is an abelian group when l | k(k−1)" (repeated in Sec. 4.2: "if l|k·(k−1), then (Z,⊙_{l,k}) forms a group"). This is false: via x↦lx+k the operation is conjugate to ordinary multiplication on a subset of Z, which has no inverses (e.g. for l=1,k=0, ⊙ is ordinary multiplication on Z). At best it is a commutative monoid/semigroup.

The theorem uses Z* = Z\{0} ("E_t is a left ideal of K(βZ*,⊙_t)") and the proof "Choose n ∈ Z* such that n^{-1}A ∈ q". The zero element of (Z,⊙_t) is t, not 0: n⊙_t x = t(t+1)−tn+(n−t)x degenerates to the constant t when n=t, so the conclusion "A is again additive piecewise syndetic" fails for n=t. The correct restriction is Z\{t}. Moreover Z* is not even closed under ⊙_t (e.g. for t=2, 1⊙_2 4 = (1−2)(4−2)+2 = 0), so (βZ*,⊙_t) is not a semigroup. Also the proof writes A = n⊙_t B, whereas only n⊙_t B ⊆ A holds.

The proof picks s among {t_1,…,t_n} with C = s^{-1}A additively central and writes A = s⊙_t C = t(t+1)−ts+(s−t)·C. If s = t this is the singleton {t} (since t is the zero of ⊙_t), so the argument gives no information; the case s=t is not excluded. Also the equality A = s⊙_t C should be an inclusion s⊙_t C ⊆ A.

The proof concludes h̃[(E(K(βZ,+))) ∩ E(K(βZ,·))] = (E(K(βZ,⊕_t)) ∩ E(K(βZ,⊙_t)), which omits the closure operators present in the theorem statement h̃[cl(E(K(βZ,+))) ∩ E(K(βZ,·))] = cl(E(K(βZ,⊕_t))) ∩ E(K(βZ,⊙_t)). The displayed conclusion therefore does not prove the stated theorem.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1, definition of the set L
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: L = {p : (∀A∈p)(∀F∈P_f(P))(∃a,d∈Z)(∀p∈F) a+p(d)∈A} omits the requirement d ≠ 0. Since every polynomial in P has zero constant term, taking d=0 and any a∈A satisfies the condition trivially, so as written L = βZ and all subsequent statements about L (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.8(3)) are vacuous. (The polynomial van der Waerden theorem requires d≠0.) The letter p is also used simultaneously for ultrafilters and polynomials.

After setting F' = {1/(n−t) f : f ∈ F}, the proof asserts the existence of a,d with a + (1/n)P(d) ∈ n^{-1}A. The factor must be 1/(n−t) (equivalently, one should write a + P(d) with P∈F'), since n⊙_t(a + (1/(n−t))P(d)) = t(t+1)−tn+(n−t)a + P(d) = c + P(d). With the factor 1/n the claimed identity n⊙_t(a+P(d)) = c+P(d) does not hold. The proof also writes "{n : n^{-1}A ∈ q} ⊆ p" where it should be "∈ p".

The proof is internally incoherent: it writes "Choose F_1·x_1 ⊂ A*" using ordinary multiplication instead of ⊙_t and treating a containment as a choice; it writes "choose F_{N+1} ∈ D*" although F_{N+1} is a finite set from the Rado family (should be F_{N+1} ⊆ D*); and it ends with the dangling, unconnected sentence "This completes the induction. a sequence such that σ_t(⟨x_n⟩_n) ⊂ B." Conclusion (1) "⟨F_n⟩_n ⊂ A" is also a type error (a sequence of sets is not a subset of A; it should be ∪_n F_n ⊆ A).

"In [4], authors proved for every finite partition of Z, there exists two sequences ⟨x_n⟩, ⟨y_n⟩ such that FS(⟨x_n⟩_n) ∪ FP(⟨x_n⟩_n) is monochromatic." The displayed set uses the SAME sequence for FS and FP, which is the well-known open problem (monochromatic FS and FP of one sequence); the text itself says two sequences, so the second term must be FP(⟨y_n⟩_n). As written the cited result is misstated and claims an open problem.
The statement says "there exist t ∈ Z, and three sequences ⟨x_n⟩, ⟨y_n⟩, ⟨z_n⟩, and ⟨w_n⟩" — four sequences are listed (and four are used in the conclusion/proof), contradicting "three".

Two defects: (i) the proof defines h(x)=x−t, which is a ring isomorphism onto (Z,⊕_{-t},⊙_{-t}), but then states "from Theorem 3.4, h̃(p) ∈ cl(E(K(βZ,⊕_t))) ∩ E(K(βZ,⊙_t))" with the wrong index t instead of −t; (ii) it concludes "(t + FS_{-t}(⟨y_n⟩)) ∪ (t + σ_{-t}(⟨z_n⟩)) ⊆ A − t", which double-shifts: from A−t ∈ h̃(p) one gets FS_{-t}(⟨y_n⟩) ⊆ A−t, i.e. t+FS_{-t}(⟨y_n⟩) ⊆ A, as the theorem's monochromaticity claim requires.

"In this section we give an affirmative answer to [11, Final remarks (4)]" — reference [11] is Hindman's 1974 JCTA paper on finite sums, which has no "Final remarks (4)". The abstract and introduction correctly attribute this question to [7] (Di Nasso). Internal citation inconsistency.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 4.10 and Corollary 4.12 ("In particular for l = 1; k = −1")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: For l=1, k=−1 one gets c⊙_{1,−1}d = lcd + k(c+d) + (k²−k)/l = cd − c − d + 2, NOT cd + c + d. Hence "a+b = 2(cd+c+d)" (Thm 4.10) and "x+P(y−x) = z+w+zw" (Cor 4.12, also in the abstract) correspond to l = 1, k = 1, not k = −1. The stated parameter value is wrong.

Theorem 4.8, on which the partition-regularity results rest, explicitly assumes l ≠ 1 ("If l (≠ 1), k ∈ Z such that l | (k−1)"), yet Theorems 4.10–4.12 state the hypothesis merely as l | (k−1) and then instantiate the special case l = 1, which is excluded by the tool being used (for l=1 the affine map n⊙_{1,k}x degenerates when n = −k, exactly the case the restriction l≠1 was introduced to avoid).

Item 1(b) claims "if A is a syndetic set in (Z,⊙_{l,k}), then A is syndetic in (Z,+)", with proof "similar to the proof of Theorems 3.3, 3.5". But Theorem 3.5 only obtains additive PIECEWISE syndeticity, and the text itself calls it a "weaker result" compared to [3, Theorem 6.1] (multiplicatively syndetic ⟹ additively central, which also only gives piecewise syndetic). The stronger syndeticity conclusion is neither proved nor supported by the cited analogue.

Item 3 asserts "L is a left ideal in (βZ, ⊙_{l,k})" on all of βZ, while the analogous Theorem 4.3 (whose proof it claims to copy) is stated only for (βZ\Z, ⊙_t), i.e. nonprincipal ultrafilters; the proof of 4.3 genuinely needs p nonprincipal to pick n avoiding the degenerate value. The strengthened statement is unsupported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Corollary 4.14 (statement and proof) and proof of Corollary 4.12
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Corollary 4.14 writes the right-hand sides as y_1 ⊕_{l,k} y_2 ⊕_{l,k} ⋯ ⊕_{l,k} y_n, and the proof of Corollary 4.12 writes "x+P(y−x) = z ⊕_{l,k} w"; the symbol ⊕_{l,k} is never defined (only ⊕_t = a+b−t and ⊙_{l,k} are defined), and the intended operation is clearly ⊙_{l,k}. In addition, Corollary 4.14 never quantifies l,k nor assumes l | (k−1), and its variables x, y in P_i(y−x) are undeclared (and the necessary condition x ≠ y from Cor. 4.12 is dropped).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1, after Definition 2.3, and proof of the (unnumbered) Theorem 3.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "a set A is thick iff there exists a left ideal L such that L ⊆ A" and "A is syndetic iff for every left ideal L, L ∩ A ≠ ∅" confuse subsets of S with subsets of βS: left ideals consist of ultrafilters, so the correct statements involve the closure Ā = {p ∈ βS : A ∈ p}. The same type error is propagated in the proof of Theorem 3.1 ("there exist a left ideal L such that L ⊆ A. But then h(L) = L + t ⊆ A + t", and "h̃^{-1}(M) ∩ A ≠ ∅").

"We call such a family, a Rado family if every additive or multiplicative piecewise syndetic subset of Z contains a member of Z." As written the definition is meaningless (it should read "contains a member of F"); the proof of Theorem 4.5 indeed uses the intended meaning (F_1 ∈ F with F_1 ⊆ A*).

The statement involves t (σ_t, f ⊙_t y, A+t) but t is never quantified in the hypothesis ("Let p ∈ cl(E(K(βZ,+))) ∩ E(K(βZ,·)), and A ∈ p"); the conclusion is therefore ill-posed without "for every t ∈ Z".
